paper.title: Revisiting the "Push-T" Robot Manipulation Task with Agentic Robotics
paper.central_claim: A frontier coding agent (Claude Code with Fable 5), prompted to write a code-as-policy for Push-T and allowed to iterate against the simulator without demonstrations, produced a procedural controller that reaches 100% success (97.2% with a vision pipeline) over 200 seeds with 46% fewer steps than the public LeRobot diffusion-policy checkpoint (62.5%), then self-improved on an agent-written Push-Alphabet A-Z benchmark to 99.4% (650 episodes) and ported to Franka/UR5e simulations.
paper.claim_scope_note: Short case study; 2D gym_pusht plus agent-authored Push-Alphabet and 3D sims; no real robot; one agent trajectory; ~221 h with human interaction and $1,500-2,000 API cost.
paper.scope_decision: in_scope (A-class): frontier coding agent iteratively writes and revises robot controllers against simulator feedback (embodied harness self-optimisation / code-policy revision).

G.reason: The question (can a coding agent author a demonstration-free procedural Push-T controller, and how does it compare with a diffusion policy) is a reasonable case study, and classical neighbours are named (Dubins re-implemented, CRISP cited). But no concrete failure of existing agentic/code-as-policy systems is identified and the agentic neighbours [7-9] are not positioned, so the residual is thin (anchor 2).

M.reason: The generated controllers (contact library, quasi-static model, MPC, digital-twin friction adaptation) are described, but the evaluated method is the agentic loop, for which no hypothesis about why it succeeds is offered; success may owe to simulator-source access, human prompts or training-data familiarity, and information access is described inconsistently (found the sim online vs no web search). Anchor 2.

X.reason: Prompts and loop stages are listed and the benchmark is specified, but code/policies are not provided, human interaction within 221 h is unquantified, the task-spec visibility level behind Tables 1-2 is unstated, and version promotion/curriculum choices are narrated rather than specified. Anchor 2 (main steps described, key conditions unclear).

measurement.reason: Coverage-based environment success over 200 seeds and 650 episodes, DP re-evaluated and sanity-checked against 65.4%. Held at 2: the vision row 97.2% is impossible over exactly 200 binary trials, the Push-Alphabet suite and 3D simulators (i.e. the success checkers) were written by the evaluated agent, which also read simulator source, the success criterion is described inconsistently (0.9 vs "identical" to gym_pusht 95%), and the visibility level is unstated.

causality.reason: DP and a refined classical Dubins baseline exist, but the headline mixes information (privileged state vs image), interaction budget (unlimited sim, ~221 h, $1.5-2k vs 200 demos), simulator-source access and human steering; v1->v3 improvement has no control; agent/model not varied. Anchor 2.

holdout.reason: Push-Alphabet final numbers are on the suite used for curriculum and exams (dev = test); Push-T seed overlap with development unstated; all gym episodes share one fixed goal pose (agg:A01); the Franka/UR5e ports run in agent-authored simulators with unknown tuning, labelled preliminary. Only weak partial holdout.

statistics.reason: Episode counts but no CI or variance; the unit of the central claim (the agentic run) has n=1 with admitted prompt sensitivity; failure analysis is one sentence; one reported percentage is arithmetically impossible. Anchor v2: no repeats of the claimed unit and no failure decomposition -> <=1.

cost.reason: 9.5M output tokens, $1,500-2,000 and ~221 h disclosed. Not 4: no stage breakdown, human effort unquantified, DP demonstration/training cost not on the same scale.

status.reason: Complete fixed HTML full text with appendix read; all eight items resolved.

resolutions.reason: A case-study question without an identified failure of existing agentic/code-as-policy systems and without positioning against the agentic neighbours is anchor 2; sol's reason concedes no closest-source verification.

The paper explains the produced controller, not the loop it claims as the method; key assumptions (no reliance on simulator internals, human steering, prior knowledge) are untested and information access is inconsistently described.
Sol itself lists incomplete promotion/visibility boundaries; with code absent and human share unquantified, the loop cannot be rebuilt beyond its main stages (anchor 2).

Son55 missed that 97.2% is impossible over exactly 200 trials; with agent-authored success checkers (agent also read simulator source) and the 0.9-vs-identical criterion inconsistency, the verifier is not independent of the evaluand (EVIDENCE rule 3 spirit).

The self-learning gain (47.1 -> 99.4%) is measured on the very suite/seeds used for exams (dev = test, close to the anchor-0 case); gym goal pose is fixed; the only partial holdout (3D ports) is agent-built with unknown tuning.
Anchor v2: the claimed unit (agent run) is unrepeated and failure decomposition is one sentence -> <=1; an impossible percentage further weakens the statistics.
